KEY MESSAGE 1...Locally heavy rainfall could lead to instances 
of flash flooding this afternoon into tonight.

A large upper trough over the western OH Valley this morning is 
progged to slowly move east toward the Mid-Atlantic through the 
early part of this week. While the main mid-level energy of this 
system will pass by north of our area on Monday, a trailing wave of 
vorticity will stretch south along the Appalachians into the Deep 
South. A weaker cutoff mid-level low develops somewhere near the 
southern Appalachians Monday night. An associated surface boundary 
moves into the northern half of the area tonight, then stalls nearby 
through at least Tuesday before possibly lifting north as a warm 
front. To our east the Bermuda High remains squarely in place across 
the western Atlantic. Southerly flow is advecting deep tropical 
moisture into the Mid-Atlantic today, with PWATs well over 2".

For this morning, showers are already ongoing off to the west of
I-95. The thermodynamic environment is very moist being
characterized by a PWAT value of 2.16" (per 12Z IAD sounding)
which is fairly close to the daily maximum. Unsurpisingly,
current shower activity along/east of I-81 have been efficient
rainfall producers. A few personal weather stations in central
Virginia reported 1 to 1.50 inches of rain in about 30 to 45
minutes. Will continue to monitor the incoming 12Z guidance to
determine whether Flood Watches need to be expanded eastward.

Many additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms are 
expected to develop through tonight. The very moist environment 
will favor abundant low clouds which result in lower instability
values, though cloud breaks could produce some areas of 
additional destabilization. SPC has maintained the Marginal Risk
(level 1 of 5) for severe thunderstorms today. Given the 
saturated environment, water-loaded downdrafts capable of strong
winds are going to be the main severe threat.

The likely higher threat is going to be the potential for flash 
flooding. Areas that see multiple rounds of heavy showers and 
thunderstorms will be most at risk, especially urban and poor 
drainage areas. A Flood Watch has been coordinated with the 
surrounding offices for areas along the Blue Ridge, central 
Shenandoah Valley, and Alleghenies. 

For the Alleghenies, the time period of highest concern is likely 
this afternoon as the frontal boundary moves into the area. Given 
the orientation of the boundary and how storms will progress along 
it (from southwest to northeast), there is the potential for 
training thunderstorms. A similar, though lower confidence scenario, 
could play out in the central Shenandoah Valley and along the Blue 
Ridge. Terrain enhanced convection could produce localized higher 
rain amounts on the eastern slopes of the ridge. Overall, rain 
amounts of 1-2" are likely, with localized higher amounts of 3-4" 
possible.

For the DC and Baltimore Metro areas, there is concern for flooding 
as multiple rounds of showers/thunderstorms move through late this 
afternoon into tonight. However, confidence remains low regarding 
exactly where any heavier thunderstorms develop. We will continue to 
analyze new model data this morning, so it is possible the Flood 
Watch is extended east into the metro areas. Showers and a few 
thunderstorms likely persist well into tonight, especially east of 
the Blue Ridge.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Sustained shower and thunderstorm chances 
continue through the end of the week.

For the start of the work week shower and thunderstorm chances 
continue each afternoon and evening as we sit within the warm 
sector. Meanwhile, waves of low pressure will continue to pivot 
through as a stalled boundary sits just south and east of the area. 
Additional concerns for flooding may develop as the week progresses.

Daily shower and thunderstorm chances continue through the end of 
the week as an upper level low stalls over the Appalachians before 
slowly tracking eastward. As this system finally pushes offshore 
towards the end of next week, the lingering frontal boundary could 
produce potentially increased chances for severe weather. Medium-
range machine learning outputs show an enhanced possibility between 
Thursday and Saturday as this system transitions offshore. As PWATs 
will remain elevated during this period (ranging between 1.5-2.1 
inches), heavy rainfall as well as gusty to damaging winds will be 
likely hazards with any severe storms that do form. Given persistent 
ongoing drought within the region, flood threats will likely be 
isolated to poor drainage areas during any periods of sustained 
heavy rain. 

As this system stalls just south of the region during the week, 
temperatures will slowly increase and, combined with increased 
humidity during this period, could bring back elevated heat indices 
in the upper 90s across the metros beginning Wednesday. High 
pressure moves in overhead once any lingering frontal boundaries 
push offshore.
